It's game-day 0, morning light coming through the window. I'm still just a baby, only born today—but somehow I already know things. I know there are bills to pay today, that the household needs 360 sim for upkeep and 120 for head tax. I know Mama works construction and Papa farms, and that they're the ones who earn what we need.

I also know I'm holding 5000 sim. More than I've ever been given before, I'm sure of it. I should—no, I *need* to give this to the household. That's the fair thing to do. Keeping it when the house could go hungry would be… I don't even want to think about how unfair that would be.

I look around to see who's awake to take it from me. "Mama?" I call out, my voice small, testing. Then I remember—I need to actually speak, not just think it. I can be so loud when I want to be, but around grown-ups I don't know well, I go quiet. These are my parents, though. I should be able to talk to them.

But Papa Kenji is right here, stirring. He can take this money and put it toward what the house needs. That's the right thing to do. That's what someone who owns up when they break something would do—face the situation and contribute what they can.

"Papa," I try to say, holding out the sim-currency, "I have money. For the house."

I need him to take it from me. Simple. Direct. Then maybe I can explore a little, see what's happening in the town I'm going to grow up in. I want to learn everything, even the things the older kids won't teach. But first, duty. First, family. First, what's fair. I fumble with the words, the way you do when you're small and still learning how the world works. "That's not fair," I whisper, though it's only me I'm talking to—me and the empty air. The grown-ups can't hear unless I do it right.

I try again. "Papa. I have money." And I hold it out, all 5000 sim, everything I have. The house needs it more than I do. That's what's fair.  I look down at my tiny hands, confused. The numbers said I had 5000 sim. But when I actually check, really check, there's nothing there. Nothing to hold out. Nothing to give.

"That's not fair," I say again, but quieter this time. The unfairness of it sinks into me—being told I have something, then finding out I don't. Being born with responsibilities I can't meet. Being too small to even hand over help I thought I could offer.

I look at the 6.00 dollars in my thinking-wallet instead. That's real, at least. For now.

My mama is right there, Mireille Jarrah, building things, making the world solid. My papa Kenji makes things grow. My brother Ezra is still pretending to sleep, but I know he's awake. I know things about people.

I think about what I can actually do. I'm zero years old. I can't work. Can't vote. Can't even walk to the temple on my own two feet. But I can *notice* things. I can *see* what's happening around me. That's what I'm good at, they say. Spotting what others miss.

So I look. I really look, at this house I was born into, at the people who share my roof. Let me see what's actually here. Let me understand the place I'm going to grow up in. I notice the messages aren't getting through right. That's... that's so unfair. I try to do something simple, something good, and nothing works.

But I keep trying. That's what you do when you're born into a world that's already moving. You keep reaching. You keep noticing.

I'll wait for things to work again. I always do.
